title: The Economics of Attention in Museums
paras: Walk through any major art museum and time how long visitors spend in front of each painting. Studies that have done precisely this find the median to be somewhere between fifteen and thirty seconds — less time, often, than it takes to read the wall label. Museum professionals tend to treat this figure as an indictment, either of a distracted public or of institutions that have failed to make their collections engaging. But the statistic may tell us less about attention than about the structure of the museum visit itself.

Consider the problem from the visitor's side. A large museum may display several thousand works across dozens of rooms. A visitor with two hours, a finite supply of energy and an uncertain sense of what is worth seeing faces a classic allocation problem. Spending ten minutes with each painting would allow them to see perhaps a dozen; spending fifteen seconds allows them to survey hundreds. Under these conditions, rapid browsing is not a failure of attention but a rational search strategy — a way of sampling widely in order to identify the few works that merit closer engagement.

The evidence supports this reading. When researchers look beyond the median, they find that dwell times are highly unequal: most works receive a glance, but a small number receive several minutes from a substantial share of visitors. The pattern resembles foraging more than neglect. Visitors skim until something catches them, then stop. What matters, on this view, is not the average time per painting but whether each visitor finds at least a few works that hold them.

This reframing has practical implications. Museums that respond to short dwell times by adding more text, more audio guides and more interactive screens may be making the search problem harder rather than easier, adding to the volume of material visitors must process. Some curators have experimented with the opposite approach: showing fewer works, with more space between them, and encouraging visitors to choose a handful of objects to study closely. Early results suggest that visitors in such displays report greater satisfaction, even though they see less.

None of this means that the fifteen-second glance is ideal. A glance at a Rembrandt is not an experience of a Rembrandt. But the remedy may lie less in exhorting visitors to slow down than in designing spaces that make slowing down a natural consequence of finding what one came, often without knowing it, to find.

qs.s: The author's main purpose in the passage is to:
o: argue that museum visitors have become less attentive than in the past.
reinterpret short average viewing times as a rational search strategy and consider its implications for museum design.
criticise museums for displaying too many works of art.
explain why Rembrandt's paintings attract more attention than other works.
qs.e: The passage reframes the dwell-time statistic (paras 2–3) and draws design implications (para 4). A is the view the author challenges. C is one implication, too narrow. D misreads the Rembrandt reference, which is illustrative.

qs.s: The author uses the word 'foraging' (paragraph 3) to suggest that visitors:
o: are primarily motivated by hunger and fatigue.
sample widely and stop when they find something that rewards attention.
avoid works of art that they consider unfamiliar.
follow a predetermined route through the museum.
qs.e: The metaphor describes skimming until something 'catches them', then stopping. A literalises the metaphor; C and D are not suggested.

qs.s: According to the passage, adding more text and interactive screens to galleries may:
o: significantly increase visitor dwell times.
make it harder for visitors to identify works worth close attention.
be the most effective way to engage younger visitors.
reduce the number of visitors to museums.
qs.e: Para 4 says such additions 'may be making the search problem harder'. A contradicts this; C and D are not mentioned.

qs.s: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's interpretation of short dwell times?
o: Visitors who browse quickly report finding a few works they remember vividly.
Dwell times are roughly equal across all works, with almost no paintings receiving extended attention from any visitor.
Museums with fewer works on display report higher visitor satisfaction.
Most visitors spend about two hours in a museum.
qs.e: The author's reading rests on unequal dwell times — glances for most works, long stops for a few. Uniformly short times would undermine the foraging interpretation. A and C support the author; D is neutral.

qs.s: The author's attitude toward the fifteen-second glance can best be described as:
o: wholehearted approval.
contemptuous dismissal.
qualified understanding.
indifferent neutrality.
qs.e: The author explains why the glance is rational but concedes in the final paragraph that it 'is not ideal' — qualified understanding. A ignores the concession; B ignores the defence; D ignores the clear argument.

title: Urban Trees and the Inequality of Shade
paras: Few urban amenities seem as innocent as a street tree. Trees cool the air, absorb stormwater, reduce noise and, by most accounts, make neighbourhoods more pleasant places to live. Yet the distribution of urban tree cover in many cities is strikingly unequal. Satellite analyses of American cities have found that wealthier neighbourhoods often have far more canopy than poorer ones, and that the difference can translate into surface temperatures several degrees higher in the least-shaded districts during summer heat waves.

Part of the explanation is historical. In many cities, neighbourhoods that were denied mortgage lending in the early twentieth century — a practice known as redlining — remain less green today. Lacking investment, these areas saw fewer trees planted and maintained, and were more likely to be cleared for highways, industry and dense housing. The legacy persists because trees take decades to mature: a planting decision made in the 1930s shapes the canopy of the 2020s.

Planting more trees in under-shaded neighbourhoods would seem to be the obvious remedy, and many cities have launched ambitious programmes to do just that. But these programmes have encountered unexpected resistance. Some residents worry about the costs of maintenance, falling branches, or roots that damage pavements. Others fear, with some justification, that greening a neighbourhood will raise property values and rents, displacing the very residents the trees were meant to benefit — a phenomenon researchers have begun to call 'green gentrification'.

These concerns suggest that the problem cannot be solved by planting alone. Successful programmes tend to involve residents in choosing where trees go, commit the city to long-term maintenance rather than leaving it to homeowners, and pair greening with protections against displacement, such as rent stabilisation or community land trusts. Trees, in other words, are not merely environmental infrastructure; they are embedded in the same economic and political forces that shape everything else in the city.

As heat waves grow more frequent, the stakes of this question will only rise. Shade may come to be seen not as an amenity but as a public health necessity — and its unequal distribution as a matter of justice rather than aesthetics.

qs.s: The central concern of the passage is:
o: the scientific benefits of urban trees for climate and stormwater management.
the unequal distribution of urban tree cover, its historical roots, and the complications of remedying it.
the history of redlining in American cities.
the rising cost of maintaining urban trees.
qs.e: The passage covers inequality, historical cause, resistance to remedies and successful approaches — B. A is only the opening context; C is one cause; D is one concern among several.

qs.s: According to the passage, the legacy of redlining persists in tree cover partly because:
o: redlining is still practised in many cities.
trees take decades to mature, so past planting decisions shape present canopy.
residents of redlined areas oppose all tree planting.
highways were built only in wealthy areas.
qs.e: Para 2: 'The legacy persists because trees take decades to mature'. A is false per the passage; C overstates para 3; D reverses the passage.

qs.s: 'Green gentrification', as described in the passage, refers to:
o: the planting of trees in wealthy neighbourhoods.
the displacement of existing residents when greening raises property values and rents.
resistance to tree planting due to maintenance costs.
the conversion of industrial land into parks.
qs.e: Para 3 defines it as greening raising property values and displacing residents. A, C and D describe other phenomena.

qs.s: The author would most likely agree that a tree-planting programme in an under-shaded neighbourhood would be most effective if it:
o: planted as many trees as possible as quickly as possible.
left maintenance responsibility entirely to homeowners.
involved residents and included measures to prevent displacement.
focused only on reducing summer temperatures.
qs.e: Para 4 lists resident involvement, city maintenance and anti-displacement measures. A and D ignore the complications; B contradicts the passage.

qs.s: In the final paragraph, the author suggests that shade may increasingly be viewed as:
o: an aesthetic luxury.
a public health necessity and a matter of justice.
a source of conflict between residents and cities.
less important than air conditioning.
qs.e: The final sentence states this directly. A is the view it moves away from; C and D are not suggested.

title: The Myth of the Learning Style
paras: Ask a room of teachers whether students learn better when instruction matches their preferred 'learning style' — visual, auditory or kinaesthetic — and most will say yes. The idea is intuitive, widely taught in teacher-training programmes and enthusiastically endorsed by students themselves, many of whom can tell you confidently which type of learner they are. It is also, according to a substantial body of research, almost entirely unsupported.

The key test of the learning-styles hypothesis is straightforward. Identify students' preferred styles, randomly assign them to instruction that either matches or does not match those preferences, and measure what they learn. If the hypothesis is correct, students should do better when instruction matches their style. Reviews of the research have found very few studies that use this design at all, and those that do generally find no such benefit. Visual learners do not learn more from diagrams than auditory learners do; both benefit from diagrams when the content is spatial.

This last point hints at what actually matters. The best way to present material depends far more on the material than on the learner. Geography is best taught with maps, music with sound, and a tennis serve with practice, regardless of anyone's stated preference. Moreover, students who are taught in multiple modes — seeing, hearing and doing — tend to learn more than those taught in any single mode, because each representation reinforces the others.

Why, then, does the myth persist? Part of the answer is that people do have genuine preferences, and it is easy to mistake a preference for an aptitude. A student who enjoys diagrams may engage more with them, but that is not the same as learning more from them. Another part is that the idea flatters both teachers and students: it promises a personalised key to every mind, and it offers a ready explanation for failure that does not implicate effort.

Debunking the myth is not merely an academic exercise. Time and money spent assessing learning styles and tailoring lessons to them is time and money not spent on practices with strong evidence behind them, such as spaced repetition and retrieval practice. The harm of the learning-styles myth lies less in what it does than in what it displaces.

qs.s: The passage is primarily concerned with:
o: explaining how to identify a student's learning style.
arguing that the learning-styles hypothesis lacks support and diverts resources from effective practices.
proving that all students learn in exactly the same way.
describing the history of teacher-training programmes.
qs.e: The passage tests the hypothesis, finds it unsupported, explains its persistence and notes its opportunity cost — B. A contradicts; C overstates (the author accepts preferences exist); D is irrelevant.

qs.s: According to the passage, the best way to present material depends mainly on:
o: the learner's stated preference.
the nature of the material being taught.
the teacher's own learning style.
the age of the students.
qs.e: Para 3: 'depends far more on the material than on the learner'.

qs.s: The author distinguishes between a 'preference' and an 'aptitude' in order to:
o: explain why students' genuine likes may be mistaken for evidence that matching instruction improves learning.
argue that students' preferences should be ignored entirely.
show that visual learners are more common than auditory learners.
suggest that aptitude cannot be measured.
qs.e: Para 4 uses the distinction to explain why the myth persists. B overreaches; C and D are not supported.

qs.s: Which of the following findings would most strengthen the author's argument?
o: Students who prefer diagrams spend more time looking at them.
A randomised study finds that matching instruction to learning style produces no improvement in test scores.
Most teachers believe in learning styles.
Students enjoy lessons tailored to their preferred style.
qs.e: The author's case rests on the absence of a matching benefit in properly designed studies; B adds such evidence. A and D concern preference, not learning; C concerns belief, which the author already acknowledges.

qs.s: The final sentence, 'The harm of the learning-styles myth lies less in what it does than in what it displaces,' means that:
o: learning-styles instruction actively damages students' ability to learn.
the main cost of the myth is the opportunity cost of neglecting more effective methods.
the myth has displaced older, worse theories of learning.
teachers who believe the myth should be replaced.
qs.e: The preceding sentence explains that resources spent on learning styles are not spent on evidence-backed practices — opportunity cost. A contradicts 'less in what it does'; C and D misread 'displaces'.

title: Why Ships Got Bigger
paras: In 1956, an American trucking entrepreneur named Malcolm McLean loaded fifty-eight aluminium boxes onto a converted tanker in New Jersey and sent them to Texas. The shipping container was not, strictly speaking, a new idea — various forms of standardised cargo boxes had been tried before — but McLean's insistence on a system in which the same box moved seamlessly between ship, truck and train transformed global trade. Before containerisation, loading a ship was a labour-intensive process that could take days, with cargo handled piece by piece by teams of dockworkers. Afterwards, a crane could lift a box from a truck onto a ship in minutes.

The economic effects were profound but not immediate. For more than a decade, ports, unions, shipping lines and railways resisted the new system or failed to adapt to it. Containers required massive investments in specialised cranes, ships and port facilities, and they rendered entire categories of dock labour obsolete. It was only when standards for container sizes and fittings were agreed internationally in the late 1960s that the system's full advantages could be realised.

Once those standards were in place, the logic of scale took over. A ship carrying twice as many containers costs far less than twice as much to build and operate, so shipping lines competed by ordering ever-larger vessels. The largest container ships today carry more than twenty thousand boxes. Ports that could not dredge deep enough channels or build large enough cranes found themselves bypassed, while a handful of mega-ports grew into global hubs.

Economists still debate how much containerisation contributed to the explosion of world trade in the late twentieth century. Some studies suggest that it did more to boost trade than all the tariff reductions of the period combined. Others caution that it is difficult to separate its effects from those of other changes, such as cheaper communications and the opening of China to the world economy.

What is clear is that the humble box changed the geography of production. When shipping goods across oceans became cheap and predictable, manufacturers could split production across continents, sourcing components wherever they were cheapest. The global supply chain, for better and worse, is in large part the container's creation.

qs.s: Which of the following best describes the structure of the passage?
o: A problem is described, several solutions are evaluated, and one is recommended.
An innovation is introduced, its slow adoption and subsequent effects are traced, and its broader significance is assessed.
Two competing theories are compared and the author sides with one.
A historical myth is described and then refuted.
qs.e: The passage introduces containerisation, explains resistance and standardisation, traces scale effects and assesses impact — B.

qs.s: According to the passage, the full advantages of containerisation were realised only after:
o: McLean's first voyage in 1956.
international standards for container sizes and fittings were agreed.
China opened to the world economy.
the largest container ships were built.
qs.e: Para 2 states this explicitly.

qs.s: The passage suggests that ports which could not accommodate very large ships:
o: became global hubs.
were bypassed in favour of mega-ports.
benefited from reduced competition.
were nationalised by governments.
qs.e: Para 3: such ports 'found themselves bypassed'.

qs.s: The author's treatment of the debate over containerisation's effect on trade (paragraph 4) can best be described as:
o: dismissive of studies that credit containerisation.
balanced, presenting a strong claim alongside a caution about isolating causes.
strongly supportive of the view that tariffs mattered more.
uninterested in economic evidence.
qs.e: The author presents both the strong claim and the methodological caution without resolving it — balanced. A, C and D misrepresent the tone.

qs.s: The phrase 'for better and worse' in the final sentence implies that the author:
o: considers global supply chains entirely beneficial.
recognises that the global supply chain has both benefits and drawbacks.
believes containerisation should be reversed.
thinks the container's effects were negligible.
qs.e: The phrase signals mixed effects. A and C pick one side; D contradicts the passage.

title: The Return of the Repair Shop
paras: For much of the twentieth century, repairing broken goods was an ordinary part of life. Radios, shoes, toasters and clothing were mended at home or by local tradespeople, and products were often designed to be opened and fixed. Over recent decades, that culture has largely disappeared in wealthy countries. Goods have become cheaper relative to labour, so that replacing an item often costs less than paying someone to repair it. At the same time, many products have become harder to fix: components are glued rather than screwed together, spare parts are unavailable, and repair manuals are kept confidential.

Manufacturers offer several justifications for designs that resist repair. Sealed devices can be thinner and more water-resistant. Restricting repairs to authorised technicians, they argue, protects consumers from shoddy work and protects the safety of products such as batteries. Critics counter that these justifications often mask a commercial interest: a product that cannot be repaired must be replaced, and a repair monopoly allows manufacturers to charge high prices for their own services.

A growing 'right to repair' movement has challenged these practices. Advocates have pushed for laws requiring manufacturers to make spare parts, tools and repair information available to consumers and independent repair shops. The European Union and several American states have passed such laws in recent years, covering products from smartphones to farm tractors. Farmers, in fact, have been among the movement's most effective advocates, since a tractor that cannot be repaired during harvest because of software locks can mean a ruined crop.

The environmental argument for repair is strong. Manufacturing a new smartphone, for example, accounts for the large majority of the device's lifetime carbon emissions, so extending its life by even a year or two yields significant savings. Electronic waste is among the fastest-growing waste streams in the world, and much of it contains toxic materials.

Yet laws alone may not revive repair culture. The skills once common among ordinary people and local tradespeople have faded, and repair remains expensive where labour costs are high. Some cities have responded with 'repair cafés', volunteer-run events where people bring broken items and learn to fix them together. Whether such initiatives can scale beyond enthusiasts remains to be seen.

qs.s: The passage is mainly concerned with:
o: the history of the smartphone industry.
the decline of repair culture, the debate over repairability, and efforts to revive repair.
the environmental impact of farming equipment.
why manufacturers make thinner devices.
qs.e: B captures the full arc. A, C and D are narrow details.

qs.s: According to the passage, one reason repair declined is that:
o: people lost interest in owning durable goods.
goods became cheap relative to the cost of labour.
governments banned independent repair shops.
products became more water-resistant.
qs.e: Para 1 states this. C is not mentioned; D is a manufacturers' justification, not a cause of decline; A is unsupported.

qs.s: The author mentions farmers primarily to:
o: show that the right-to-repair movement concerns only consumer electronics.
illustrate how restrictions on repair can have serious practical consequences, making farmers effective advocates.
argue that tractors are more important than smartphones.
criticise farmers for relying on software.
qs.e: The example shows high stakes — a ruined crop — explaining farmers' advocacy. A contradicts; C and D are unsupported.

qs.s: The author's view of manufacturers' justifications for repair-resistant design is best described as:
o: fully accepting of them.
presenting them alongside critics' argument that they often serve commercial interests.
dismissing them as entirely dishonest.
indifferent to them.
qs.e: Para 2 presents both justifications and the critics' counter — B. C overstates ('often mask', not always).

qs.s: The final paragraph suggests that:
o: right-to-repair laws have fully revived repair culture.
legal reforms may be insufficient because repair skills have faded and labour remains costly.
repair cafés have replaced professional repair shops.
repair is no longer environmentally beneficial.
qs.e: The final paragraph states 'laws alone may not revive repair culture' and explains why. A contradicts; C overstates; D contradicts para 4.
